prompt: Which protocols does Microsoft Entra ID use to prove identity, where Active Directory uses Kerberos?

choices.text: Kerberos too, over the internet
choices.why: Kerberos is the local network's protocol; Entra ID speaks the web's.

choices.text: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SAML
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: LDAP, with a certificate
choices.why: LDAP is how programs query Active Directory, not how Entra ID signs people in.

choices.text: NTLM, through a proxy in the office
choices.why: NTLM belongs to Active Directory's local world.

prompt: What is wrong with "Entra ID is our Active Directory, moved to the cloud"?
hint: Compare what each was built for.

choices.text: Nothing: it is the same product under a new name
choices.why: Only the old name was shared. The two are different directories.

choices.text: Entra ID runs on domain controllers the company owns
choices.why: Active Directory does; Entra ID is a service in Microsoft's cloud.

choices.text: Entra ID replaces Active Directory, so the office's servers can be switched off
choices.why: In a company running both, the office's file server still asks Active Directory.

choices.text: They are two directories built for different worlds
choices.why: Right. One for machines on a network, the other for applications on the internet.

prompt: A synchronised user's surname is misspelt. An administrator corrects it in Entra ID. What happens?
hint: Where is the source of authority?

choices.text: Entra ID refuses the edit
choices.why: The lesson's point is what happens after it is made.

choices.text: The correction is written back to Active Directory
choices.why: Writeback covers a few things such as passwords, not a surname edited in the copy.

choices.text: The next synchronisation puts the misspelling back
choices.why: Right. Change a synchronised account in its source, Active Directory.

choices.text: The user is split into two accounts
choices.why: Nothing splits; the copy is simply overwritten.

prompt: Copying something from Entra ID back to Active Directory, such as a password reset in the cloud, is called ___.
hint: A word for the direction it travels.

prompt: A leaver is disabled in Entra ID only, on a Friday evening. Which risk remains, by the lesson?
hint: Which directory do the office's machines ask?

choices.text: The person can still log in to the office's machines
choices.why: Right. And the next synchronisation may even enable the cloud account again.

choices.text: The account is deleted in Active Directory by the next cycle
choices.why: Synchronisation does not delete on the ground what the cloud disabled.

choices.text: None: disabling in Entra ID disables everywhere
choices.why: Entra ID is the copy; Active Directory is not told.

choices.text: The person's emergency account stays active
choices.why: Emergency accounts are not per person; there are two, for the tenant.

prompt: In Cloud Sync, what is installed in the company's network?

choices.text: The whole engine, with its database
choices.why: That is Connect Sync.

choices.text: A light provisioning agent
choices.why: Right. The configuration and the processing live in Entra ID.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Something must read Active Directory from inside the network.

choices.text: A domain controller run by Microsoft
choices.why: Microsoft runs no domain controller in the company's network.

prompt: How often, in minutes, does Connect Sync run a synchronisation cycle by default?
Why does the lesson call a synchronisation server "the kind of machine everybody forgets"?
hint: What happens the week it stops?

choices.text: Because it needs no updates once installed
choices.why: It needs patching and upgrades, which is the problem.

choices.text: Because Microsoft runs it for you
choices.why: Connect Sync runs on the company's own server.

choices.text: Because it has no logs
choices.why: Logs exist; the trouble is nobody looking at them.

choices.text: It runs quietly until it stops, and then nobody new can sign in
choices.why: Right. Which is why the lesson says to monitor it as a service.

prompt: Match each statement to the synchronisation program it describes.
hint: One keeps a database on the ground; the other keeps its engine in the cloud.

pairs.left: several active agents fail over on their own
handles several forests and every writeback

prompt: A company acquired two small firms, each with its own simple Active Directory, and wants all three in one tenant with no new server to run. What does the lesson point to?
hint: Which one suits several small directories?

choices.text: Connect Sync, because only it reads more than one directory
choices.why: Cloud Sync handles several disconnected directories; Connect Sync is for complex joins.

choices.text: Federation, since it needs no synchronisation
choices.why: Federation decides who checks passwords; the accounts still have to be copied.

choices.text: Cloud Sync, with agents in each directory
choices.why: Right. Simple directories, several of them, and no engine to host.

choices.text: Three tenants, one per firm
choices.why: That splits identity instead of joining it.

prompt: With password hash synchronisation, who checks the password at sign-in?
hint: Nothing on the ground is needed.

choices.text: Entra ID, against the synchronised hash
choices.why: Right. The office can be down and people still sign in.

choices.text: A domain controller, through an agent
choices.why: That is pass-through authentication.

choices.text: The company's AD FS servers
choices.why: That is federation.

choices.text: Nobody: the hash replaces the password
choices.why: The person still types a password, and it is checked.

prompt: Why does Microsoft advise a company using pass-through authentication to sync password hashes as well?

choices.text: Because pass-through only works for administrators
choices.why: It works for every synchronised user.

choices.text: Because the agents need the hashes to talk to Active Directory
choices.why: The agents pass the typed password to Active Directory; they need no hash.

choices.text: A fallback if the agents fail, and the leaked-credentials report
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because Entra ID refuses sign-ins without a hash
choices.why: Pass-through works without hashes; they are a fallback.

prompt: Which need does pass-through authentication answer that password hash synchronisation does not?

choices.text: Enforcing a just-disabled account at once
choices.why: Right. Hash sync waits for the next cycle.

choices.text: Signing in when the office is offline
choices.why: The opposite: pass-through needs the office; hash sync does not.

choices.text: Reporting passwords found in leaks
choices.why: That report needs the hashes in the cloud.

choices.text: Signing in with no password at all
choices.why: All three methods here are about checking a password.

prompt: `getuserrealm.srf` answered `Managed` for `microsoft.com`. What does that tell you?

choices.text: Microsoft's tenant has no on-premises directory
choices.why: The answer is about where passwords are checked, not about what Microsoft runs on the ground.

choices.text: Its people sign in with cloud authentication, not federation
choices.why: Right. A federated domain would answer `Federated`.

choices.text: The domain is unknown to Entra ID
choices.why: That answer is `Unknown`, which `shop.example` got.

choices.text: The domain is managed by a partner company
choices.why: Managed is Entra ID's word for cloud authentication.

prompt: Why does the shop choose password hash synchronisation?
hint: Fewer servers between a person and Azure.

choices.text: Because federation is no longer supported by Entra ID
choices.why: Federation is supported; staged rollout exists to move away from it at a company's pace.

choices.text: Because it stores the passwords so they can be recovered
choices.why: No password is stored in a reversible form.

choices.text: Because it enforces account changes the fastest
choices.why: It is the slowest of the three at that.

choices.text: No requirement needs the others, and fewer servers can fail
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Put the path of a new employee at the shop in order, from HR to signing in to Azure.
hint: The account is born on the ground.
items: HR's process creates the account in Active Directory
a Cloud Sync agent reads it when the service asks
the person types a password at Microsoft's sign-in page
Entra ID checks it against the synchronised hash
trap: The copy has to exist before any sign-in can find the person.

prompt: Which of these need something running in the company's network for a person to sign in to Azure? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Password hash synchronisation
choices.why: The check happens in Entra ID.

choices.text: Pass-through authentication
choices.why: Right. The agents and the domain controllers.

choices.text: Federation with AD FS
choices.why: Right. The federation servers.

choices.text: An emergency access account
choices.why: Cloud-only, on purpose.

prompt: Which part of this lesson ran in the lab?
hint: One request to a public address.

choices.text: Asking Entra ID how two domains sign in
choices.why: Right. `getuserrealm.srf`, which answers anybody.

choices.text: A sign-in with password hash synchronisation
choices.why: No sign-in was attempted.

choices.text: A Cloud Sync cycle against a test directory
choices.why: There is no directory in the lab.

choices.text: Reading Connect Sync's database
choices.why: There is no Connect Sync server.
